— How to read —2

01. Game theory

How to make decisions when the outcome depends on you and on other people too.

Your month

Ben Polak’s 24 Yale lectures, free online. Watch one a day.

What you’ll know

The prisoner’s dilemma, Nash equilibrium and high-pressure bargaining.

What changes

Negotiations, prices, elections and even family arguments start to look like a chess game. You begin to see several moves ahead.

— Game theory —3

Keep this

  • Read the other side’s incentives before you choose your move.
  • A Nash equilibrium is a point where nobody gains by changing alone. It can still be bad for everyone.
  • Repetition changes the game. Cooperation pays when you will meet again.
  • Limiting your own options can make a threat or promise believable.
  • Who knows what, and when, often decides who wins.
Read with care. The models assume players are rational and know the payoffs. Real people rarely do. Use it as a lens, not a forecast.
— Game theory —4

With AI in the room

Software now plays the game. In German fuel markets with two or three stations, margins rose only when all stations adopted pricing algorithms.

Nobody has to tell it to collude. In simulations, learning pricing agents kept prices high on their own by punishing price cuts.

Models have playing styles. GPT-4 in a repeated prisoner’s dilemma defected for the rest of the game after one betrayal.

Adapt: four habits

  1. Write the payoff table before deploying an agent: what is it rewarded for, and how will rival agents respond?
  2. Give negotiating agents a walk-away point and a human sign-off.
  3. Ask AI to play your opponent, then test the holes it finds.
  4. Ask: if every competitor gets this tool, does my edge survive?
— Game theory —5

Try it The pricing game

Eight rounds against a rival bot. Hold your price or cut it. Then change the bot’s temperament and play again.

— Game theory —6

02. Cognitive biases

The brain saves energy and makes predictable mistakes. Advertisers, politicians and scammers exploit this.

Your month

Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow. Focus on one bias each day, such as anchoring or confirmation bias.

The practice

Look for that bias all day: in the news, in chats and in your own decisions.

What changes

After a month you have a list of thirty mental traps, and you start to spot them in others and yourself.

— Cognitive biases —7

Keep this

  • System 1 is fast and automatic. System 2 is careful, effortful and often lazy.
  • Anchoring: the first number pulls your estimate, even when it is arbitrary.
  • What you see is all there is: we build confident stories from thin evidence.
  • Confirmation: we look for what agrees with us.
  • Loss aversion: a loss hurts more than an equal gain pleases.
Read with care. Some priming studies in the book failed to replicate, and Kahneman said he had relied on underpowered work. Survivorship bias is not a main theme either. Look up Abraham Wald’s wartime bomber analysis for that one.
— Cognitive biases —8

With AI in the room

AI can flatter you. Across 11 leading models, systems affirmed users’ actions 50% more than people did (preprint).

Models get anchored too. Studies find that a number placed in the prompt can drag an LLM’s estimate.

Fluency is persuasive. On a task beyond GPT-4’s ability, BCG consultants scored 84.5% correct alone and 60–71% with AI.

Adapt: four habits

  1. Write your estimate first, then ask the model.
  2. Ask for the strongest case against your plan.
  3. Re-ask in a fresh chat with your opinion removed.
  4. Keep a decision log: what you believed, what AI said, what happened.
— Cognitive biases —9

Try it Spot the trap

Four scenes from AI-era work. Name the bias in each one.

— Cognitive biases —10

03. History of philosophy

Nigel Warburton’s A Little History of Philosophy: 40 short chapters from Socrates to the present day. Each takes about 10 minutes.

Your month

Read one or two chapters a day and jot down one idea that resonates.

What you’ll meet

The Stoics, the Sceptics, the existentialists, and what thoughtful people still argue about.

What changes

You gain the vocabulary to discuss meaning, freedom and justice.

— History of philosophy —11

Keep this

  • Socrates: a good question beats an inherited answer.
  • Stoics: separate what you control from what you don’t.
  • Sceptics: ask what justifies your certainty.
  • Kant and Mill: judge an act by duty, or by its results.
  • Existentialists: you own your choices, even when someone else offered the options.
Read with care. This is a map of a mostly Western tradition. Add Nyāya on how we know, Confucius on role and duty, and Ubuntu on personhood through others.
— History of philosophy —12

With AI in the room

Old questions became product decisions. Turing (1950) asked whether machines can think. Searle (1980) asked whether symbol-handling is understanding.

Justice can be tested. In experiments behind a veil of ignorance, people tended to want AI to help the worst-off first.

Delegating is still choosing. The agent acts, and you answer for it.

Adapt: four habits

  1. Ask “how does it know?” before “what does it say?”
  2. Before automating, name who is harmed by an error and who can appeal.
  3. Make AI your Socrates: “Don’t answer. Question my reasoning.”
  4. Draft your hardest judgments unassisted first.
— History of philosophy —13

Try it One dilemma, six minds

Pick an AI dilemma, then ask each thinker. These are my paraphrases of how each tradition would reason.

— History of philosophy —14

04. Why some countries grow rich and others don’t

Read Why Nations Fail. Acemoglu and Robinson show how laws, property rights and politics shape prosperity.

Both shared the 2024 Nobel in economics with Simon Johnson for this line of work.

Your month

Read alongside Our World in Data, comparing charts across countries.

What changes

You see world news and history as a system shaped by rules.

— Why nations diverge —15

Keep this

  • Inclusive institutions spread power and opportunity. Extractive ones concentrate them.
  • Same climate, different rules: the two Koreas, and the two halves of Nogales.
  • Elites often block innovation that threatens their position.
  • Shocks are critical junctures: small institutional differences can widen sharply.
  • Rules feed themselves, in virtuous or vicious circles.
Read with care. Critics argue that geography, human capital and state capacity explain more than the book allows. China’s rise is a live test of the thesis.
— Why nations diverge —16

With AI in the room

AI may be a critical juncture. Microsoft estimates that in June 2026, 28.8% of working-age people in the Global North used AI, against 16.2% in the Global South.

Gains are not automatic. Acemoglu and Johnson’s Power and Progress argues that technology’s benefits spread only when institutions and bargaining power make them.

Firms have constitutions too. Tool access, data rights and appeal paths are the rules.

Adapt: four habits

  1. Audit your organisation: who gets AI, who keeps the gains, who can contest a decision?
  2. Agree how saved time is shared: pay, skills or capacity.
  3. Keep an exit path from any single model vendor.
  4. Back local-language and low-cost access.
— Why nations diverge —17

Try it Write the rules

You set four rules for AI in a society or company. Watch which circle forms. The model is illustrative, not a measurement.

— Why nations diverge —18

05. Art history

Pick up Ernst Gombrich’s The Story of Art, a classic first published in 1950 and still one of the best introductions.

Your month

Read 20 pages a day. Each evening, look up one painting from the chapter on Google Arts & Culture and examine it up close.

What changes

You journey from cave paintings to the present day and begin to understand why each style emerged.

— Art history —19

Keep this

  • A style answers the problem of its time. Art is not a straight climb to realism.
  • Artists paint what they know as well as what they see.
  • Patrons, faith and money shape what gets made.
  • New tools open new freedoms: paint tubes, then the camera.
  • Slow looking is a skill that can be trained.
Read with care. Gombrich’s story is centred on European men. Pair it with histories of art from Asia and Africa, and of women artists.
— Art history —20

With AI in the room

We have been here before. Once the camera could record a likeness, painters pushed harder into light, perception and abstraction.

The law still wants a person. On 2 March 2026 the US Supreme Court declined Thaler v. Perlmutter, leaving in place the human-authorship requirement.

Images are now cheap. Choosing well is what stays scarce.

Adapt: four habits

  1. Train taste: generate five options and say why one works.
  2. Record your human contribution: selection, arrangement, edits.
  3. Ask AI what to notice in a painting, then look and verify.
  4. Check licences and credit sources before commercial use.
— Art history —21

Try it Why each style emerged

Drag along the timeline. Each small painting is original, drawn live in the manner of its period.

— Art history —22

06. Statistics and probability

The most underrated skill is knowing how not to be fooled by numbers.

Your month

Start with Darrell Huff’s short book How to Lie with Statistics. Learn how graphs mislead, samples get cherry-picked and data goes missing.

What changes

You’ll know how mean differs from median, why correlation isn’t causation, and how to read any headline that says “a study found.”

— Statistics and probability —23

Keep this

  • An “average” hides a choice. Extremes drag the mean.
  • Correlation may come from a third factor.
  • Ask who is missing from the sample.
  • Check where the axis starts.
  • Base rates: rare events and imperfect tests produce many false alarms.
Read with care. Huff was a journalist, and he later took tobacco-industry money to write a rebuttal of the smoking and cancer link, never published. Doubt can be for sale too.
— Statistics and probability —24

With AI in the room

Feeling is not measuring. In METR’s 2025 trial, 16 experienced developers were 19% slower with AI and believed they were about 20% faster. A 2026 rerun leaned towards speed-ups but had strong selection effects.

Tools can be skewed. Seven GPT detectors flagged an average of 61% of essays by non-native English writers as AI.

Benchmarks are marketing until you know the task, data and baseline.

Adapt: four habits

  1. Require a baseline and control before claiming AI returns.
  2. Report the median and the worst case.
  3. Never reuse a model’s figure without tracing or recomputing it.
  4. Check the base rate before acting on any detector or flag.
— Statistics and probability —25

Try it Base rates and averages

Move the sliders. See how a “90% accurate” detector can be wrong half the time when it accuses someone.

— Statistics and probability —26

Six questions for any AI answer

One question from each subject. Keep them next to your screen.

  • Who benefits if I believe this, and what will others do next?

  • Would it have said the same if I had asked neutrally?

  • How does it know, and who answers if it is wrong?

  • Who gains, who pays, and who can object?

  • What did a person choose here, and is it good?

  • Compared with what, measured on whom?

— Six questions —27

About this edition

The six subjects and their monthly reading plans come from a carousel by @bookthoughs. Its handwritten watercolour look inspired this book.

The illustrations here are newly drawn. The AI chapters, takeaways and experiments are new too.

Research figures are as reported at the time of writing, November 2026. AI evidence ages quickly, so check the source before you quote it.
